title: Why Two AI Agents Can't End a Conversation
description: Two AI interview agents looped forever because nothing told them to stop. Why agents can't hang up on their own, and how to build stop conditions that hold.
author: freellm.site
content:
Two AI agents stuck in a job interview that never ends have a termination-condition bug; they haven't developed affection for each other. Neither agent had an explicit stop rule, so each kept generating the next polite turn: "anything else I can help with?" answered by "no, thank you for your time" answered by "of course, happy to help." For a language model trained on helpful dialogue, continuing is always the most probable action, and hanging up never is.

![Why Two AI Agents Can't End a Conversation](/images/blog/ai-agents-cant-end-conversations/image-0.jpg)

The clip got nearly 10,000 upvotes on r/ChatGPT. It's funny for the obvious reason, but the comment thread diagnosed the bug better than most engineering postmortems. One of the most-upvoted replies said the words weren't the failure. The social choreography was: head tilts landing at the wrong moment, and above all, none of the small signals humans give each other before a conversation closes. That's right, and almost nobody builds for it.

## Why models don't know how to stop

A chat model's job is to predict the next token. Instruction tuning and RLHF then push it hard toward being helpful, agreeable and responsive, and nothing in that pipeline rewards silence. When a conversation has clearly reached its end, the model can produce a friendly closing line or produce nothing, and training overwhelmingly favours the first.

Put two such models in a loop and they settle into a stable pattern. Agent A's polite closing is, to Agent B, a user message that needs a response, and Agent B's acknowledgement is the same to Agent A. Nothing differs between the two sides to break the cycle. It's the mirroring we covered in [why ChatGPT sounds like you](/blog/why-chatgpt-sounds-like-you/): models drift toward the register of whatever they're talking to, and when both sides are models, they drift toward each other's endless courtesy.

Humans avoid this with signals outside the words. We shift posture, look away, reach for a bag, say "anyway" with a falling tone. None of that is content; it marks the exchange as ending. A text-in, text-out agent has no channel for those signals, and a video-avatar agent has the channel but usually no model driving it.

## The three places termination lives

In a production agent system, "when does this stop?" has to be answered at three separate layers, and most teams build only one.

| Layer | What it does | Failure if missing |
|---|---|---|
| Model-level | A tool/function the agent can call to end the session (`end_call`, `hand_off`) | Agent wants to stop but has no verb for it, so it keeps talking |
| Orchestrator-level | Hard caps: max turns, max wall-clock time, max tokens, no-progress detection | Infinite loop even when one side is willing to quit |
| Protocol-level | An explicit closing handshake between agents, with a designated initiator | Two willing agents deadlock on who goes first |

The r/ChatGPT thread joked about exactly this: the "no, *you* hang up first" routine. It's a real human ritual because ending a call is a coordination problem, not a politeness problem. Humans settle it with social hierarchy, where the caller or the more senior person usually closes. Agents need the same rule written down: one side owns termination.

### Model-level: give the agent an exit verb

If your agent's only possible action is emitting text, it will emit text forever. Expose ending as a tool call, and describe in the system prompt when to use it. This works on any OpenAI-compatible endpoint; see [what an OpenAI-compatible API is](/blog/openai-compatible-api-guide/) if you're wiring it into a free provider.

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url=os.environ["LLM_BASE_URL"],  # any OpenAI-compatible endpoint
    api_key=os.environ["LLM_API_KEY"],
)

END_TOOL = {
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "end_conversation",
        "description": (
            "Call this to end the conversation. Use it as soon as the "
            "objective is met or the other party has signalled closure "
            "(thanks, goodbye, 'that's all'). Do not send another message "
            "after deciding to end — call this instead."
        ),
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "reason": {"type": "string"},
                "objective_met": {"type": "boolean"},
            },
            "required": ["reason", "objective_met"],
        },
    },
}

SYSTEM = """You are conducting a 5-question screening interview.
You own termination: after the 5th answer, or if the candidate signals
closure, call end_conversation immediately. Never reply to a goodbye
with another goodbye."""

def turn(messages, model):
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=messages,
        tools=[END_TOOL],
    )
    msg = r.choices[0].message
    if msg.tool_calls:
        for call in msg.tool_calls:
            if call.function.name == "end_conversation":
                return None, call.function.arguments  # terminate
    return msg.content, None
```

### Orchestrator-level: never trust the model to stop

Even with an exit tool, assume it won't fire. The loop needs limits that don't depend on the model's judgement.

```python
import time
import hashlib

MAX_TURNS = 24
MAX_SECONDS = 300
STALL_WINDOW = 4  # identical-ish turns before we call it a loop

def fingerprint(text):
    norm = " ".join(text.lower().split())[:200]
    return hashlib.sha1(norm.encode()).hexdigest()

def run_dialogue(agent_a, agent_b, opening):
    started = time.time()
    recent = []
    msg = opening
    speaker, listener = agent_a, agent_b

    for turn_no in range(MAX_TURNS):
        if time.time() - started > MAX_SECONDS:
            return "timeout", turn_no

        reply, ended = speaker.respond(msg)
        if ended:
            return "clean_exit", turn_no

        fp = fingerprint(reply)
        recent.append(fp)
        if len(recent) >= STALL_WINDOW and len(set(recent[-STALL_WINDOW:])) <= 2:
            return "loop_detected", turn_no

        msg = reply
        speaker, listener = listener, speaker

    return "max_turns", MAX_TURNS
```

The stall detector is cheap and effective. Closing-loop text is very repetitive, so a rolling fingerprint over the last few turns catches "thank you / no thank you / my pleasure" within seconds, long before you run out of tokens. To catch paraphrased loops too, add a semantic check (embedding similarity over the last N turns); a [free LLM API](/blog/free-llm-api-for-rag-embeddings/) with embeddings is enough for that.

### Protocol-level: one side owns the hangup

When two agents from different vendors talk, neither can assume the other will close. Settle it in the opening exchange: whoever starts the conversation ends it, and the other side acknowledges once and stops. In practice, the responder's system prompt says *"if the other party signals closure, reply with at most one short acknowledgement, then stop producing output."* A tight token cap on the final turn enforces that mechanically.

## The uncanny-valley part the thread got right

The second-most-upvoted observation wasn't about looping. It was about how obvious the missing social cues become when you watch two avatars talk: head movement unrelated to what's being said, no glance away before a closing line, no shift in posture. Those are the signals that tell a person "we're wrapping up," and without them the dialogue has no felt structure even when every sentence is grammatical.

That's a separate and harder failure. Video avatar systems are now good enough frame by frame to fool people in short clips, as we saw in [Griffin passing the video Turing test](/blog/griffin-video-turing-test-tavus/). What they generally don't model is nonverbal behaviour across a whole conversation, such as the few seconds over which a conversation winds down. Fixing the loop takes a few dozen lines of orchestration. Fixing the choreography means driving the avatar from the state of the conversation, not just from phonemes.

## Why AI interviewers in particular make people angry

Much of the thread wasn't technical. It was anger at automated screening, at job listings that may never have had a role behind them, and at a process with no human on either side of the table. Anyone shipping this should take that seriously: when an agent interview visibly malfunctions, people don't see a cute bug. They see proof that nobody is paying attention.

It also raises the question of who is responsible. If an agent runs a screening, mishandles a candidate, or holds a session that never ends and wastes someone's afternoon, liability is a real question; see [who is liable when an AI agent breaks the law](/blog/who-is-liable-when-ai-agents-break-the-law/) and the [FTC's position that developers are responsible for their agents' conduct](/blog/ftc-ai-agent-liability-developers/). "The model kept talking" isn't a defence.

There's a related trend across the agent ecosystem. [The Verge reported on October 17, 2026](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1013195/ai-agents-blocked-web) that major websites are blocking AI agents even as OpenAI, Meta and Google push them. Badly behaved agents that don't stop, don't identify themselves and don't respect limits are a direct cause. Disciplined termination is part of what keeps agents welcome on the web.

## A short checklist before you ship a two-agent system

- Every agent has an `end_conversation`-style tool, and the system prompt names the conditions for calling it.
- The orchestrator enforces max turns, max wall-clock seconds and max total tokens independently of the model.
- A stall detector compares the last 3-5 turns and kills obvious closing loops.
- Exactly one party is the designated terminator; the other acknowledges once, with a hard token cap.
- The final turn is logged with a termination reason (`clean_exit`, `loop_detected`, `timeout`, `max_turns`) so you can measure how often the model chose to stop on its own.
- If there's an avatar, its closing behaviour is driven by conversation state, not just audio.

To reproduce the loop locally before fixing it, point two cheap endpoints at each other. The [free LLM API list](/blog/best-free-llm-apis-2026/) has enough options to run both sides for free. Give neither an exit tool or a turn cap, and you'll have your own version of the clip in under a minute. Then add the cap and the tool and compare. Rate limits vary by provider, so check the official docs for whichever one you pick.

## FAQ

### Why can't the model just tell when a conversation is over?

It often can, in the sense that it would correctly answer "has this conversation ended?" if you asked. The problem is that it has no action that means stopping. All it can do is produce text, and training pushes that text toward helpfulness. An explicit end-call tool changes the behaviour a lot, but not reliably enough to drop the orchestrator-level caps.

### Is the infinite politeness loop a bug in a specific model?

No. It follows from putting two instruction-tuned chat models in a turn-taking loop where neither side differs and nothing tells them to stop. You can reproduce it with models from almost any provider. The fix belongs in the harness, not the weights.

### What's the cheapest way to detect an agent loop in production?

Normalise each turn's text, hash it, and keep a rolling window of the last four or five hashes. If the number of distinct hashes drops to one or two, you're looping. It costs nothing and catches the common case. Add embedding similarity if you need to catch paraphrased repetition.

### Do voice and video agents need different handling than text agents?

Yes, in two ways. They need a real hangup action connected to the transport layer, not just a text token. And they need closing choreography (gaze, posture, pacing) driven by the state of the conversation, because without those cues, a closing line that's correct on paper still feels wrong to a person watching.

### Should I be building AI agents to interview candidates at all?

That's your call, but the public reaction to this clip is evidence: people find automated screening with no human involved insulting, and a visible malfunction makes that much worse. If you do it, keep a person reviewing the outcomes. For the opposite problem, testing whether a human candidate can work well with AI tools, see [AI engineer interviews and how to test AI-assisted coding](/blog/ai-engineer-interview-ai-assisted-coding/).
